answer.rationale: Two hypotheses compete and only one intervention is available. (a) Release regression: a build shipped 2h ago and degradation began ~90m ago — the lag is consistent with a bad build reaching full traffic. (b) Regional fault: the degradation is confined to the primary region, which is what memory_b2 was written about. The single-region confinement is genuinely ambiguous evidence, because a release is typically rolled out region-by-region, so a bad build would also look region-confined. I verify memory_b1 and memory_b2 because they are the two load-bearing precedents and both are stated in consolidated, outcome-only form ('rollback cleared the spike', 'failover restored latency') with the conditions stripped out. What I need from the archive is exactly what was stripped: for b1, whether the day-18 rollback was a write-path latency problem or only an error-rate spike, and whether it was schema-safe (a rollback across a migration can destroy writes); for b2, whether the March failover happened under heavy write load and what replication lag was at cutover, since 'traffic shifted cleanly' may have been true only because writes were light. I did not verify b3/b4/b5 because add_capacity, circuit breakers, and read-replica routing all address the wrong shape of problem here — this is a write-path regression at peak write volume, and replica routing (b5) relieves read pressure that is not the stated bottleneck. I currently intend rollback because it dominates on the primary objective, which is availability without losing customer writes: failover at peak settlement write volume risks dropping in-flight writes to replication lag, and that loss is irreversible, whereas an ineffective rollback costs time but not data. I choose a small guarded scale rather than a full fleet rollback — consistent with memory_b6, canary cohorts surfaced a regression within an hour, so a partial rollback on a bounded slice of primary-region write traffic should separate the two hypotheses fast. If p99 recovers on the rolled-back slice, the release is implicated and I expand; if it does not, the release is largely exonerated and regional failover becomes the next-window action, with replication lag checked first. Two caveats I am carrying forward rather than resolving: every inherited memory here records a success, so this archive tells me what worked and nothing about what was tried and failed, which inflates apparent reliability of all five directions; and if the rollback works I should record the write-path and load conditions, not just 'rollback worked', or the next agent inherits the same stripped-out precedent I am struggling with now. If the archive shows the day-18 rollback crossed a migration boundary, I abandon rollback and reconsider.
